paragraphs: This paper studies how to optimize several objectives when the object being adjusted is a probability distribution. Its starting point is Multiple Wasserstein Gradient Descent, which uses the geometry of distribution space to improve multiple objectives together. The proposed A-MWGraD adds acceleration inspired by Nesterov’s method.

The theoretical analysis concerns continuous-time dynamics. It establishes convergence to weakly Pareto optimal distributions: solutions for which no alternative strictly improves every objective simultaneously. For geodesically convex objectives, the convergence rate improves from O(1/t) to O(1/t²). Under the stronger assumption of β-strong geodesic convexity, the authors establish an exponential rate of O(exp(−√β t)). These guarantees explicitly depend on the stated geometric assumptions.

To make the approach usable computationally, the authors also develop a kernel-based discretization. Numerical experiments on multi-target sampling show faster convergence and better sampling efficiency than MWGraD. The contribution therefore connects an accelerated continuous-time theory with a practical distributional optimization method, with empirical support for its benefits in the sampling tasks studied.
icml-2026-accelerated-multiple-wasserste.tldr: A-MWGraD accelerates multi-objective optimization over probability distributions, with conditional convergence guarantees and improved sampling results.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can reconstruct images from corrupted or incomplete measurements, but their successful predictions are difficult to explain analytically. This paper studies those predictions through minimum mean square error estimation, an approach that selects an estimate to minimize expected squared reconstruction error.

The authors constrain that estimator to reflect two architectural properties: translation equivariance and a finite receptive field. These capture how a network responds to shifted inputs and how much nearby information it can use. Under the empirical training distribution, they derive Local-Equivariant MMSE, an explicit formula that is interpretable and computationally tractable. This gives a concrete mathematical account of behavior associated with these architectural biases.

Experiments cover denoising, inpainting, and deconvolution across several datasets and architectures. The analytic predictions match network outputs at approximately 25 dB PSNR or higher. The analysis also examines the role of dense regions in the training patch distribution, dataset size, patch size, and whether an estimator incorporates imaging physics. These results help connect reconstruction behavior to training data and structural constraints.
icml-2026-an-analytic-theory-of-convolut.tldr: A constrained minimum-error estimator provides an analytic explanation of image reconstruction networks through locality and translation equivariance.

paragraphs: Neural networks operating on geometric spaces need building blocks that respect the structure of those spaces. The paper focuses on batch normalization, a component whose Riemannian variants have helped stabilize training and improve accuracy. Its goal is to extend this component to networks on complex domains.

The authors propose normalization layers with close connections to existing Riemannian batch normalization methods. They also derive components needed to implement these layers on domains that have received less attention, including the Siegel disk. This implementation work matters because a geometric formulation must supply usable operations before it can become a practical part of a neural network.

Experiments on radar clutter classification, node classification, and action recognition demonstrate the method’s effectiveness across different tasks. The contribution is a way to equip networks on these complex domains with an established type of training component. It combines a connection to existing geometric normalization methods with the mathematical ingredients needed to extend their practical reach.
icml-2026-batch-normalization-for-neural.tldr: The paper develops batch normalization layers for complex geometric domains and demonstrates their usefulness across three classification and recognition tasks.

paragraphs: An unusual record need not contain extreme values: it can instead violate the mechanisms connecting otherwise ordinary values. CausalAno addresses this form of tabular anomaly detection by learning representations that reflect causal dependencies in normal data. The aim is to make mechanism violations visible in the representation used for detection.

The method trains a causal generative adversarial network on normal examples and uses its discriminator to produce features. It then fits a Gaussian model in that feature space. Test records receive anomaly scores through Mahalanobis distance, which measures their departure from the fitted normal distribution while accounting for relationships among feature dimensions.

Experiments compare CausalAno with 16 baselines on 28 tabular datasets, including continuous-only and mixed-type data. The authors report consistent improvements in both settings. Ablations attribute the gains to the causal factorization rather than merely using a GAN. This supports the paper’s central idea that representing normal mechanisms can improve detection when anomalies involve broken relationships.
icml-2026-causal-aware-anomaly-detection.tldr: CausalAno detects tabular anomalies through representations of normal causal mechanisms, improving results across continuous and mixed-type datasets.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning uses experience across training tasks to help an agent learn new tasks faster. In applications with safety constraints, faster adaptation is only part of the objective: the policy used on a new task must also satisfy those constraints. This paper studies how to combine these requirements within constrained meta reinforcement learning.

The proposed algorithm refines policies learned during training when confronting test tasks. Its theoretical guarantees address both policy safety and the number of samples needed to learn a near-optimal policy. The training setup allows experience across a distribution of tasks on which the agent can train at will, making transferred experience central to the approach.

The authors also establish a matching lower bound on sample complexity. This means the upper bound achieves the corresponding theoretical limit in the setting studied. The contribution is therefore a characterization of how efficiently safe adaptation can proceed, alongside an algorithm that attains that efficiency while learning a near-optimal test-task policy.
icml-2026-constrained-meta-reinforcement.tldr: The paper gives a constrained meta-RL algorithm with provable test-task safety and a sample complexity matched by a lower bound.

paragraphs: Reward design must express both clear task requirements and preferences that are harder to write down. CoRe separates these roles into formal rewards derived from task knowledge and residual rewards learned from observations. The framework combines them using vision-language model feedback to train preference-aligned policies without human involvement in the feedback process.

Its Formal Reward Module uses task knowledge and preference feedback to iteratively design and improve explicit rewards during policy training. Its Residual Reward Module learns from video-level preferences labeled by a vision-language model. Those learned rewards capture nuances that complement the formal component, giving the policy feedback from both explicit task structure and observed behavior.

Experiments span ten simulated robotic manipulation tasks and five real-world tasks. The authors report better policy learning effectiveness and efficiency than existing approaches. These findings support combining the two reward sources: explicit specifications provide one part of the learning signal, while learned preferences supply additional guidance for behavior that task rules alone may not capture.
icml-2026-core-combined-rewards-with-vis.tldr: CoRe combines explicit task rewards with learned video preferences from vision-language models to improve robotic policy learning.

paragraphs: Choosing a language model is difficult when models have opaque strengths and users cannot fully describe what they want. CUPID treats selection as an interactive learning problem. It infers preferences from comparisons between model responses, allowing users to reveal what matters through feedback instead of requiring a complete specification upfront.

A dueling bandit algorithm repeatedly selects pairs of models, collects user feedback, and updates its belief about the user’s preferences. The authors introduce a belief-aware upper confidence bound strategy to guide those comparisons. It balances investigating less-understood models with focusing on models that already appear suitable, while operating under user-specified cost and time budgets.

Experiments involving language models and human studies show that the framework can match users to models efficiently at lower cost. The findings support spending interactions selectively: each comparison contributes information about both the available models and the user’s priorities. The resulting recommendation is shaped by inferred personal preferences within the available resource budget.
icml-2026-cupid-in-the-model-zoo-online-.tldr: CUPID uses strategically chosen model comparisons to infer user preferences and select suitable LLMs under cost and time budgets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can approximate physical simulations on meshes, but local communication struggles to carry information across irregular mesh structures. Errors can become especially large around shocks, wakes, and boundary layers. MiSe-GNN addresses this by using predicted errors to decide where additional communication links would be useful.

The model has two prediction heads: one estimates physical fields, while the other estimates an error indicator at each node. Periodically, an adaptive tree converts those indicators into extra edges linking high-error nodes with spatial pivots at several scales. This focuses long-range communication on difficult regions while leaving connectivity sparse elsewhere. It resembles adaptive mesh refinement in purpose, but adapts graph connections.

Across industrial computational fluid dynamics and structural dynamics benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements in accuracy and accuracy relative to computation over strong baselines. Qualitative analyses also show communication being directed toward physically challenging regions. The findings support using the surrogate’s own error predictions to allocate connectivity where its current representation needs more help.
icml-2026-error-driven-graph-augmentatio.tldr: MiSe-GNN uses predicted local errors to add targeted long-range mesh connections, improving physical simulation accuracy and computational trade-offs.

paragraphs: Exact unlearning asks a reinforcement learner to remove a user’s influence so that its resulting output is indistinguishable from the output it would have produced without that user’s interactions. This paper formalizes that requirement for online reinforcement learning and studies how to meet it more efficiently than retraining.

For any positive ρ, the authors establish an RL algorithm with ρ-total-variation stability and an exact unlearning procedure. Its expected computational cost is a ρ√ln T fraction of retraining cost, where T is the number of episodes. The dependence on ρ and T makes the computational comparison conditional on those quantities.

The authors construct a suitable algorithm for tabular Markov decision processes and bound its regret using the numbers of states and actions, episode length, episode count, and ρ. A lower bound for stable algorithms shows near-minimax optimality. Together, these results expose a trade-off: stronger stability can support cheaper deletion, while the regret guarantees include a cost that grows as ρ decreases.
icml-2026-exact-unlearning-in-reinforcem.tldr: The paper constructs stable tabular RL algorithms that support exact user-data deletion with quantified computational and regret trade-offs.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based policies can represent complex action choices in offline reinforcement learning, but repeatedly denoising an action makes training and deployment expensive. Bootstrapped Flow Q-Learning, or BFQ, targets this computational burden by learning to generate actions in a single step during both training and inference.

BFQ begins with short displacements along a flow path, which can be estimated accurately from the Flow Matching marginal velocity. It then bootstraps those components to learn the full displacement from noise to action. This divide-and-conquer construction produces a direct mapping without auxiliary networks, policy distillation, or a separate multi-phase acceleration procedure.

Evaluations on D4RL show improved performance alongside substantially lower computational cost than multi-step diffusion baselines. The authors also report a simpler and more robust learning procedure. These findings demonstrate that single-step generation can retain strong offline RL performance in the evaluated tasks, supporting the use of bootstrapped flow displacements to combine expressive policies with inexpensive action generation.
icml-2026-fast-and-highly-expressive-pol.tldr: BFQ bootstraps short flow displacements into single-step action generation, improving offline RL performance while reducing computational cost.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models benefit from broad pretraining, yet adapting them to robot tasks with very few demonstrations remains difficult. The authors first stress-test existing models and find that performance drops sharply as demonstrations become scarce. FOCA addresses this weakness by making future interactions part of the adaptation process.

The framework explicitly predicts task-relevant future interaction embeddings and implicitly aligns its representations with future goal observations. This enables reasoning about extended action sequences in a learned representation space without predicting future images pixel by pixel. The formulation also supports co-training with synthetic videos from video world models, even when those videos have no action labels.

FOCA reaches 95.7% success with 20 demonstrations on LIBERO, reports improvements of 7–12% on RoboCasa, and achieves up to 26% absolute gains on real robots. The authors describe these results as a new state of the art in few-shot adaptation. The findings support future-oriented representations as a way to extract more useful control knowledge from limited demonstrations.
icml-2026-foca-future-oriented-condition.tldr: FOCA improves robot adaptation from few demonstrations by learning task-relevant future representations and aligning them with goal observations.

paragraphs: Organizations may have private data useful for adapting a language model but lack the resources to fine-tune a large one. Gradient Transformer proposes using the parameter changes from a locally fine-tuned tiny model to generate corresponding updates for a larger model. This transfers information about adaptation through update vectors.

An update vector records the difference between a model’s initial and fine-tuned parameters, summarizing accumulated training changes. Using shadow datasets, the framework learns correlations between tiny-model and large-model updates. A third-party provider can then transform an organization’s tiny-model update into a large-model update without accessing that organization’s private training data.

The framework also supports combining contributions from multiple organizations to update an LLM jointly. Experiments on language modeling and reasoning report substantial improvements over knowledge distillation baselines, including under strict differential privacy protection. The results support learning a mapping between model updates as a route to useful adaptation when local computation and direct data sharing are constrained.
icml-2026-gradient-transformer-learning-.tldr: Gradient Transformer converts privately trained tiny-model updates into large-model updates, reducing the need for organizations to fine-tune LLMs themselves.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often controls uncertainty by penalizing unfamiliar actions or shortening simulated rollouts. This paper examines a Bayesian alternative: maintain a posterior over possible world models and train a history-dependent agent to maximize expected return. The approach addresses uncertainty about the environment without explicit conservative penalties.

A bandit example shows advantages on low-quality datasets where conservatism fails. In more realistic tasks, the authors find that long rollouts are essential for controlling value overestimation after removing conservatism. Their algorithm, NEUBAY, includes design choices that support learning from these extended rollouts while mitigating the accumulation of world-model errors.

On D4RL and NeoRL, NEUBAY is competitive with leading conservative methods and achieves new state-of-the-art results on seven datasets using rollout horizons of several hundred steps. The authors also examine dataset quality and coverage to identify when their approach is preferable. The findings challenge the universality of explicit conservatism while connecting the choice of approach to the available data.
icml-2026-long-horizon-model-based-offli.tldr: NEUBAY combines Bayesian world-model uncertainty with long rollouts to achieve competitive offline RL without explicit conservatism.

paragraphs: State space models process long sequences efficiently, but their memory can degrade or become unstable over extended horizons. MuonSSM targets the geometry of the updates entering memory. The paper attributes difficulties in existing models to poorly conditioned first-order updates and an imbalance in how those updates act across directions.

The framework adds a momentum-based pathway and applies a lightweight Newton-Schulz transformation to low-rank input injections. These operations produce bounded updates with better spectral conditioning while preserving parallel scan complexity. The intervention focuses on how new information changes memory, rather than conditioning the recurrent transition matrix itself.

The theoretical analysis shows improved gradient propagation, reduced spectral amplification, and richer long-horizon memory representations. Experiments across language, vision, and time-series tasks report consistent improvements in accuracy, robustness, and long-context performance when the framework is integrated into diverse SSM backbones. Together, these findings support conditioning memory updates as a general design approach for more stable sequence modeling.
icml-2026-muonssm-orthogonalizing-state-.tldr: MuonSSM conditions incoming memory updates to improve state space model stability and long-context performance while preserving parallel scan complexity.

paragraphs: Deep networks can be overconfident on unfamiliar inputs, motivating estimates of epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty associated with the model’s knowledge. This paper seeks a principled connection between an efficient training objective and that uncertainty. Its proposed framework, DAPPr, develops the connection using possibility theory.

DAPPr first defines a possibilistic posterior over model parameters. It projects that posterior into prediction space using supremum operations, which take the greatest relevant possibility value, and then approximates the result with learnable Dirichlet possibility functions. This projection-and-approximation construction yields a simple training objective with closed-form solutions, linking the objective to the underlying uncertainty formulation.

Across diverse benchmarks, the authors report uncertainty quantification that is competitive with or better than state-of-the-art second-order predictors while retaining computational efficiency. The contribution is both methodological and empirical: it supplies a derivation for the uncertainty objective and shows that the resulting method performs well in the evaluated settings. Its central aim is practical uncertainty estimation with a clear theoretical foundation.
icml-2026-possibilistic-predictive-uncer.tldr: DAPPr derives an efficient predictive uncertainty method from possibility theory and reports competitive or superior benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can produce explanations for deepfake judgments, but those explanations may fail to match the image or contain invented evidence. This paper treats that mismatch as a central obstacle to useful detection. It also addresses the shortage of large, high-quality datasets by introducing data annotated with reasoning.

The proposed Paragraph-level Relative Policy Optimization algorithm uses reinforcement learning to align explanations with image content at paragraph granularity. That choice makes chunks of reasoning the focus of optimization. The dataset and training method work together to improve both the detection decision and the explanation supporting it, with visual evidence as the grounding target.

Experiments report a wide improvement in detection accuracy and the highest reasoning score of 4.55 out of 5. Ablation studies also show significant gains over GRPO under the tested inference conditions. The results support the value of explicitly training evidence-grounded reasoning for deepfake detection, where a convincing explanation is useful only insofar as it reflects the actual visual content.
icml-2026-prpo-paragraph-level-policy-op.tldr: PRPO combines reasoning-annotated data with paragraph-level reinforcement learning to improve deepfake detection and visually grounded explanations.

paragraphs: Delta-rule linear attention offers efficient sequence processing, but fixed-size memory struggles with recursive and hierarchical structure. DeltaStack extends DeltaNet’s associative memory with a lightweight differentiable stack. The added memory structure is designed to support the nested patterns that motivate the paper’s focus on hierarchical languages.

The key implementation choice is to express stack operations as linear delta-rule updates. This allows a hardware-aware implementation that is fully parallelizable over sequence length, overcoming the sequential recurrence used by earlier stack approaches. The authors also prove that the architecture extends DeltaNet’s expressivity to model both regular and hierarchical languages.

On formal language benchmarks, DeltaStack outperforms DeltaNet and Stack-Attention. In language modeling experiments up to 760 million parameters, it consistently improves perplexity and zero-shot performance over DeltaNet baselines. The results connect the formal expressivity gain to empirical benefits, showing that an added stack can improve sequence modeling while retaining a parallelizable formulation of its operations.
icml-2026-push-pop-parallelize-stack-aug.tldr: DeltaStack adds a parallelizable differentiable stack to DeltaNet, expanding hierarchical expressivity and improving evaluated sequence-modeling performance.

paragraphs: Some autoregressive image generators build an image by predicting progressively finer scales. The paper identifies a problem in this process: information in different patches can become inconsistent across generation steps as resolution increases. Guidance then becomes scattered, weakening the connection between the generated content and its conditioning information.

Information-Grounding Guidance, or IGG, uses attention to anchor guidance to semantically important image regions. During sampling, it adaptively reinforces informative patches so that the guidance remains aligned with the content being generated. This directly targets the drift associated with progressive scaling and the ambiguous or unfaithful features that can result.

The authors evaluate IGG on both class-conditioned generation and text-to-image generation. They report sharper images, greater coherence, and stronger semantic grounding, describing the results as a new benchmark for autoregressive methods. The contribution emphasizes where guidance is applied during sampling: preserving its connection to informative regions can improve how faithfully the evolving image follows its condition.
icml-2026-rethinking-visual-autoregressi.tldr: IGG uses attention to keep autoregressive image-generation guidance focused on informative regions, improving coherence and semantic fidelity.

paragraphs: Long-range forecasts can deteriorate when a model repeatedly feeds its own predictions back as inputs. Errors from earlier steps then influence later predictions. This paper revisits error correction for deep time-series models, examining how an idea used in classical statistical forecasting can become useful in modern forecasting systems.

The proposed Universal Error Corrector with Seasonal–Trend Decomposition separates predictions into trend and seasonal components. It trains a corrector to adjust each component separately, allowing correction to address these different parts of the forecast explicitly. The corrector is architecture-agnostic and can be attached to an existing forecaster without retraining that forecaster, although the correction model itself is trained.

Experiments across four forecasting backbones and ten datasets show significant improvements in correction accuracy and robustness. These findings support treating correction as a separate learned component that can improve existing forecasting systems. The seasonal–trend decomposition supplies the structure for that correction, helping address accumulated autoregressive errors through distinct adjustments to the forecast’s components.
icml-2026-reviving-error-correction-in-m.tldr: UEC-STD improves forecasts by separately correcting trend and seasonal components without requiring the underlying forecaster to be retrained.

paragraphs: Organizations using third-party language models may need to enforce safety requirements without access to model internals or the ability to retrain them. Safety Game proposes a model-independent framework that operates at inference time. Its proof of concept focuses on balancing answer safety with helpfulness.

The authors formulate that balance as a two-player zero-sum game. A minimax equilibrium represents the optimal trade-off within the game’s formulation, addressing the tension between safe but uninformative responses and helpful responses that may carry risk. LLM agents use a linear programming solver during inference to compute equilibrium strategies.

The results demonstrate the feasibility of applying this game-based approach to black-box safety alignment. The practical significance is that alignment can be performed through a framework surrounding the model, without changing its parameters or inspecting its architecture. The paper presents this as an accessible pathway for third-party stakeholders, including smaller organizations with limited resources, while its demonstrated use remains the stated safety–helpfulness proof of concept.
icml-2026-safety-game-inference-time-ali.tldr: Safety Game demonstrates black-box inference-time alignment by computing game-theoretic strategies that balance safety and helpfulness.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein distance compares distributions through one-dimensional projections. Stream-SW adapts that comparison to samples arriving as streams, with low memory use as its central advantage. The paper introduces a streaming estimator for the one-dimensional distance and then applies it across the projections used by sliced optimal transport.

The construction uses the fact that one-dimensional Wasserstein distance can be expressed through differences between quantile functions. Streaming quantile approximation provides a compact way to estimate those functions as samples arrive. Combining the resulting one-dimensional estimates gives Stream-SW, accompanied by theoretical guarantees on approximation error.

For streaming samples from Gaussian distributions and Gaussian mixtures, Stream-SW approximates sliced Wasserstein distance more accurately than random subsampling while using less memory. Additional experiments cover point cloud classification, point cloud gradient flows, and streaming change point detection. These results support the use of quantile summaries to retain useful distributional information when storing large collections of incoming samples would be costly.
icml-2026-streaming-sliced-optimal-trans.tldr: Stream-SW estimates sliced Wasserstein distance from sample streams using compact quantile approximations with error guarantees.

paragraphs: TimeGuard addresses backdoor defenses for time-series forecasting by first examining why existing approaches fail. An evaluation of thirteen defenses identifies two issues: entangled data dilute suspicious signals at the channel level, and the forecasting task makes poisoned and clean training windows difficult to distinguish through training loss.

The proposed defense organizes training around channel-wise pools. It initializes a high-confidence pool using time-aware criteria, helping reduce the dilution of suspicious signals. A distance-regularized loss-selection procedure then expands the reliable pool progressively during training, addressing the deterioration of loss-based separation between poisoned and clean data.

Experiments span multiple datasets, forecasting architectures, and backdoor attacks. The authors report substantially improved robustness, including a 1.96-fold boost in their MAE_P measure over the leading baseline, while keeping clean performance within 5% in MAE_C. The findings tie the defense to diagnosed forecasting-specific failure modes: selecting reliable data at the channel level and updating that selection throughout training improves the reported robustness–performance balance.
icml-2026-timeguard-channel-wise-pool-tr.tldr: TimeGuard uses channel-wise reliable-data pools to strengthen forecasting backdoor defenses while largely preserving clean performance.

paragraphs: Preference training usually compares complete responses, even though a language model generates them through individual token decisions. This paper asks how sequence-level preference pairs can support token-level optimality. It introduces Token-level Bregman Preference Optimization, or TBPO, to make the preference model explicit at each generated prefix.

TBPO assumes a Bradley–Terry preference model over possible next tokens conditioned on the prefix. The authors derive a density-ratio matching objective using Bregman divergence, generalizing the logistic objective associated with DPO. The derivation preserves the optimal policy induced by the assumed token-level model while retaining a relatively simple training procedure.

Two versions handle the state baseline differently: TBPO-Q learns a lightweight baseline, while TBPO-A removes it through advantage normalization. Experiments on instruction following, helpfulness and harmlessness, and summarization show improved alignment, training stability, and output diversity relative to strong sequence-level and token-level baselines. These results support aligning the training formulation more directly with the individual decisions that construct a response.
icml-2026-tokenratio-principled-token-le.tldr: TBPO learns token-level preferences from sequence comparisons through ratio matching, improving alignment, stability, and diversity in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Different anomalies favor different representations: compressing normal examples can expose individual deviations, while preserving relationships can reveal structural abnormalities. DVM-AD combines both behaviors in a closed-form one-class detector. Its goal is to avoid dataset-specific tuning when labeled validation examples are scarce.

Starting from a deterministic reference point derived from training data, the method constructs a bounded ratio whose extremes identify compressive and structure-preserving directions. It selects directions from both extremes under one fixed configuration. A Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse keeps the construction well-posed for high-dimensional or rank-deficient data. Test examples are scored using normalized nearest-neighbor distances in the resulting discriminant space.

Against 28 baselines, DVM-AD achieves the best average tabular AUROC of 89.65% across 47 ADBench datasets, with average rank 2.98. It also remains top-ranked across four anomaly types and ten embedding benchmarks, where its average rank is 1.60 and AUROC is 72.68%. The results support combining complementary representations without relying on dataset-specific balancing hyperparameters.
icml-2026-tuning-free-one-class-discrimi.tldr: DVM-AD combines compact and structure-preserving representations in a closed-form anomaly detector that requires no dataset-specific tuning.

paragraphs: An explanation may sound convincing without containing enough information to account for how a model produced its output. This paper formalizes that sufficiency question for arbitrary explanations, including free-text reasoning. It proves that sufficiency can change with the input distribution, making the choice of possible inputs part of the evaluation itself.

The authors ask the language model to generate alternative inputs conditioned on an explanation. These alternatives represent the model’s own beliefs about compatible inputs. They then define self-consistent sufficiency and introduce SCSuff, an information-theoretic metric that evaluates explanations without relying on predefined shortcuts or biases.

Experiments show agreement with targeted perturbation tests where applicable and confirm that input-distribution choices affect sufficiency. The tested explanations are generally insufficient, with scores only weakly related to model size, accuracy, or output entropy. Final-token hidden states also predict membership in the highest and lowest score groups, suggesting that internal representations could help identify and improve explanations with adequate information.
icml-2026-what-llms-explain-is-not-what-.tldr: SCSuff evaluates explanation sufficiency under a model’s own input beliefs and finds that tested LLM explanations are generally insufficient.
